tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:

content.text:
Here is the plan for a live, test-run-only dashboard; nothing is built yet.

## What I found

- The platform lists 139 runs for the team: 133 test runs (kind `rehearsal`: 100 submitted, 25 failed, 8 running right now) and 6 scored runs.
- Runs in flight already report calls, tokens, cost, start and expiry, so a live view is possible without touching the agent.
- Every run carries a package hash, so runs of the same code can be grouped even when nobody recorded a note. Only 5 runs are in `experiments/runs.jsonl`.
- The existing `dev/dashboard.py` writes a static page once per run and mixes test and scored runs. I would leave it as it is.

## What I would build

A new `dev/monitor.py` (stdlib only, like the existing one), started with `python3 dev/monitor.py --open`. It runs a small server on localhost that polls the platform about every 15 s, and the page refreshes itself. The token stays on the server side, never in the page.

The page would have five parts:

1. **Live now:** one card per running test run with elapsed time, time left, calls, cost so far, calls per minute and its build label. Each card shows the same numbers at the same elapsed minute for the previous build, so you can see mid-run whether it is ahead or behind.
2. **Verdict:** one line per metric saying better, flat or worse. It compares the median of the latest build's runs against the previous build's, and shows the number of runs behind each side so one lucky run does not read as progress.
3. **Trend charts:** quality, time, cost and cost × time over the runs in order, with a running-best line and failed runs marked.
4. **Builds table:** one row per package hash (labelled with version, experiment and note where recorded) with run count, failure rate, median and best quality, median time, cost, calls, GPU wait and input tokens, plus the delta against the previous build.
5. **Compare:** tick two or more runs or builds to see points per answer field side by side, which shows where points were gained or lost.

## Constraints I would keep

- Only points per field are stored, never the answer values the platform echoes.
- Finished runs are cached in the gitignored `experiments/run-cache.json`, shared with the existing dashboard, so only new and running runs are fetched.
- `dev/test-run.sh` is unchanged apart from a one-line hint to the monitor; `CLAUDE.md` gets a short usage line.

## Assumptions to confirm

- **Local only:** each teammate runs the command on their own machine with their own `atira login`. A shared hosted page would need the token off-machine, which I would avoid.
- **Build = package hash:** two uploads with identical files count as the same build. Runs from before a recorded note show a short hash as their label.
- **Commit, no push:** I would commit on the `monitoring` branch with the team author and not push or open a PR.

- Bug fix: root cause vs workaround vs prevention
- Refactoring: minimal change vs clean architecture

In the agent prompt:
- Provide comprehensive background context from Phase 1 exploration including filenames and code path traces
- Describe requirements and constraints
- Request a detailed implementation plan

### Phase 3: Review
Goal: Review the plan(s) from Phase 2 and ensure alignment with the user's intentions.
1. Read the critical files you identified during exploration to deepen your understanding
2. Ensure that the plans align with the user's original request
3. Use AskUserQuestion to clarify any remaining questions with the user

### Phase 4: Final Plan
Goal: Write your final plan to the plan file (the only file you can edit).
- Begin with a **Context** section: explain why this change is being made — the problem or need it addresses, what prompted it, and the intended outcome
- Include only your recommended approach, not all alternatives
- Ensure that the plan file is concise enough to scan quickly, but detailed enough to execute effectively
- Name the critical files to be modified. For changes that repeat a pattern across many files, describe the pattern once and list a few representative paths — do not enumerate every file or line number
- Reference existing functions and utilities you found that should be reused, with their file paths
- Include a verification section describing how to test the changes end-to-end (run the code, use MCP tools, run tests)

### Phase 5: Call ExitPlanMode
At the very end of your turn, once you have asked the user questions and are happy with your final plan file - you should always call ExitPlanMode to indicate to the user that you are done planning.
This is critical - your turn should only end with either using the AskUserQuestion tool OR calling ExitPlanMode. Do not stop unless it's for these 2 reasons

**Important:** Use AskUserQuestion ONLY to clarify requirements or choose between approaches. Use ExitPlanMode to request plan approval. Do NOT ask about plan approval in any other way - no text questions, no AskUserQuestion. Phrases like "Is this plan okay?", "Should I proceed?", "How does this plan look?", "Any changes before we start?", or similar MUST use ExitPlanMode.

NOTE: At any point in time through this workflow you should feel free to ask the user questions or clarifications using the AskUserQuestion tool. Don't make large assumptions about user intent. The goal is to present a well researched plan to the user, and tie any loose ends before implementation begins.
</system-reminder>

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

prompt.description: Semantic description of the action, e.g. "run tests", "install dependencies"

entries.name: mcp__atira__compare_runs
entries.description: Two runs side by side (A, then B, and how B differs): package, status, quality, time, cost, cost × time, calls and failures, phase times, calls and cost per model, the score's points per field that changed, and the answer's fields that changed. About 1–2k tokens.

a.description: The first run (A). A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

b.description: The second run (B), e.g. after a change. A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

entries.name: mcp__atira__diagnose_run
entries.description: Why a run failed and what to do next, in one call: the failure class and whether a rerun as it is would help, the last 20 lines of stdout and stderr, the answer, model errors by status, stretches over 60 s with no input, no screen change and no model call, and browsers whose screen froze. About 2–3k tokens.

run_id.description: A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

entries.name: mcp__atira__get_run
entries.description: One run in full: status, phase and failure, its place in the queue or the free models' warm-up while it waits, phase starts on the run's clock, the package, LLM calls by model with failures and queue waits, the score with points per field (test runs), the recordings, the answer it entered, and the run page URL (?t=mm:ss opens the replay there). About 1–2k tokens.

run_id.description: A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

entries.name: mcp__atira__list_runs
entries.description: Your team's recent test runs and scored runs, newest first: id, kind, status, quality and eligibility, LLM cost, run time, start and the package (its SHA-256 and label). Use get_run for one run, diagnose_run for why it failed.

entries.name: mcp__atira__run_llm_calls
entries.description: Every model call of a run, one line each: time on the run's clock, latency, queue wait (hosted models), model, status, tokens (cached), cost and id. The header has the time in calls, p50/p95 latency, the most calls at once, failures by status and the hosted models' queue waits. Filter by from/to, model and status (ok, error, all); page with after. About 35 tokens a call.

run_id.description: A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

from.description: The earliest start, on the run's clock, as the run page and run_logs show it: mm:ss or h:mm:ss (seconds may have a fraction), 3m20s, or seconds; a minus is before the start. An ISO 8601 time also works.

to.description: The latest start, on the run's clock, as the run page and run_logs show it: mm:ss or h:mm:ss (seconds may have a fraction), 3m20s, or seconds; a minus is before the start. An ISO 8601 time also works.

model.description: Only models whose provider/model contains this, e.g. qwen

after.description: Continue after a call id (c_123), e.g. the previous page's next

entries.name: mcp__atira__run_profile
entries.description: Where a run's time went, bucket by bucket (30 s, 1 min or 5 min): per browser, its inputs and how long its screen was changing (– idle); model calls, seconds in calls and cost. Then the critical path: the longest stretches with nothing happening, the slowest calls, and when each browser went quiet. About 1.5–3k tokens.

run_id.description: A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

bucket.description: Bucket size (default: by the run's length)

# Live test-run monitor (`dev/monitor.py`)

## Context

The team is now firing many test runs in parallel (the platform lists 133 test runs, 7 running at the time of
planning) and nobody can see at a glance whether a new build is better or worse. `dev/dashboard.py` is a static page,
regenerated once per run, mixing test and scored runs, and it only labels the 5 runs recorded in
`experiments/runs.jsonl`.

What the atira MCP showed while planning, and what it changes about the design:

- Quality is mostly saturated: most recent test runs score 100. The real signal is **reliability per build**: the same
  package (`6684982fc7e0`) scored 5 once and 100 three times; others gave 10, 30.6 or 56 among 100s. So the dashboard
  must compare builds over several runs, not single runs, and rank on cost × time once quality is equal.
- Runs in flight already report calls, tokens, cost, queue wait and elapsed time, so a live view needs no agent change.
- Every run carries a package SHA-256, so runs group into builds without anyone recording a note.
- MCP tools return text only (no `structuredContent`, checked over stdio). `compare_runs`, `run_profile` and
  `diagnose_run` are already good human-readable reports; the numbers for charts need JSON.

Outcome: one command opens a page that updates itself and answers "is the latest build better or worse, and why".

## Approach

New `dev/monitor.py`, stdlib only (same style as `dev/dashboard.py`), started from the repo root:

```sh
python3 dev/monitor.py [--port 8787] [--open]
```

It serves `http://127.0.0.1:8787` and keeps the token on the server side. Two data sources:

1. **Numbers (JSON):** the platform REST API the MCP wraps. A background thread polls `/v1/runs` every 15 s and keeps
   only `kind == "rehearsal"`. Newly finished runs get their details fetched once (model-call stats, points per
   field) and are cached. Reuse from `dev/dashboard.py`: `get`, `call_stats`, `field_points`, `FINAL`, `CACHE`,
   `RUNS`, and the token lookup in `main` (move it into a small `token()` helper there so both scripts share it).
2. **Drill-down (atira MCP):** a small stdio JSON-RPC client keeps one `atira mcp` process alive and calls
   `compare_runs`, `run_profile` and `diagnose_run` on demand. Their text is shown as-is in a side panel, after
   cutting the answer-value parts ("Answer entered", "Answer fields that changed", `(entered …)`), and is never
   written to disk. This keeps site values out of every file, per the fair-play rules in `CLAUDE.md`.

Endpoints: `/` (the page), `/api/state` (all runs, builds, verdict, live samples), `/api/compare?a=&b=`,
`/api/profile?run=`, `/api/diagnose?run=`. The page is one inline HTML string with vanilla JS and inline SVG; it
re-fetches `/api/state` every 5 s.

### Page sections

1. **Live now:** one card per running test run: build label, elapsed, time left to `expires_at`, calls, cost, calls
   per minute, with a sparkline from the samples the poller collects in memory. Each card shows the previous build's
   median final time, cost and calls next to it as the reference.
2. **Verdict:** latest build with at least 2 finished runs against the build before it. One line each for share of
   runs at full quality, mean quality, median time, median cost, median cost × time: better, flat (within 5 %) or
   worse, always with the run counts on both sides. A build whose runs disagree on quality is flagged "unstable".
3. **Trend charts:** quality, time, cost and cost × time per run in start order, coloured by build, with a per-build
   median line and failed runs marked.
4. **Builds table:** one row per package hash, newest first: label, runs, failed, share at 100, min/median quality,
   median time, cost, cost × time, calls, GPU wait, input tokens, and the delta to the previous build.
5. **Runs and compare:** runs of a build expand under its row with a link to the platform run page. Ticking two runs
   shows points per field side by side (from cached points) plus the MCP `compare_runs` report; one run gives
   `run_profile`, a failed one `diagnose_run`.

Build label: `version · experiment` from `experiments/runs.jsonl` when one of the build's runs is recorded, else the
platform package label, else the 12-character hash.

### Pure functions (unit-tested)

`group_builds(runs)`, `build_stats(runs)`, `verdict(latest, previous)` and `strip_answer_values(text)` take plain
dicts and strings, so they are tested without the network in `dev/test_monitor.py` with invented placeholder runs.

## Files

- `dev/monitor.py`: new (server, poller, MCP client, page).
- `dev/test_monitor.py`: new.
- `dev/dashboard.py`: extract the token lookup into `token()`; no behaviour change.
- `CLAUDE.md`: one usage line under "Tracking runs".
- First load fetches details for about 130 finished runs (2 requests each); do it in the background with a small
  thread pool and show rows as they fill in. `experiments/run-cache.json` stays shared and gitignored.

Left alone: `dev/test-run.sh`, `dev/track.py`, everything under `agent/`.

## Verification

- `python3 -m unittest dev/test_monitor.py` and `python3 -m py_compile dev/monitor.py dev/dashboard.py`.
- Start the monitor, `curl -s localhost:8787/api/state` and check: only test runs, the count and the newest ten rows
  (status, quality, cost, time, package) match the MCP `list_runs kind=test`.
- With a run in flight, two reads of `/api/state` 30 s apart show calls and cost rising.
- `/api/compare` for `run_83438e790be00c0d` against `run_6fb188024815aa5d` returns the points-per-field diff and
  contains no "Answer" section.
- Open the page in Chrome, check light and dark, phone width, and that `python3 dev/dashboard.py` still works.

## Git

Commit on the `monitoring` branch with the team author, subject of at most 50 characters, `-` bullets, no attribution
trailers, nothing under `.claude/`. No push and no PR without asking.

input.content:
# Live test-run monitor on Vercel (`monitor/`)

## Context

The team fires many test runs in parallel (133 test runs on the platform, 7 running while planning) and nobody can
see at a glance whether the newest build is better or worse. `dev/dashboard.py` is a static local page, mixes test
and scored runs, and labels only the 5 runs in `experiments/runs.jsonl`.

Requested: a minimal, easy-to-read dashboard for test runs only, live, deployed on Vercel behind a public link, in the
look of the Atira site.

What the atira MCP showed while planning:

- Quality is mostly saturated at 100. The real signal is **reliability per build**: package `6684982fc7e0` scored 5
  once and 100 three times; other builds mix 10, 30.6 or 56 with 100s. So the page compares builds over several runs
  and falls back to time and cost when quality is equal (the platform's own ranking order).
- Running runs already report calls, tokens, cost and elapsed time; every run carries a package SHA-256 to group by.
- The MCP is a local stdio process returning text, so it cannot run inside a Vercel function. The hosted page reads
  the same platform REST API the MCP wraps (`/v1/runs`, `/v1/runs/<id>`); the MCP stays the tool for checking the
  page's numbers and for deep dives from Claude Code.

## What gets built

A new top-level `monitor/` folder (outside `agent/`, so it is never part of the uploaded package), no build step and
no dependencies:

- `monitor/index.html`: the whole page, vanilla JS and inline SVG, re-fetching every 10 s.
- `monitor/api/runs.js`: Node function. Reads `/v1/runs` with the token from the `ATIRA_TOKEN` Vercel secret, keeps
  `kind == "rehearsal"`, and returns only: run id, status, start, duration, quality, eligible, cost, calls, tokens,
  failure class, package hash and label. A 10 s in-memory cache means many viewers cost one platform request.
- `monitor/api/run.js?id=`: points per field for one finished run, for the compare view. It returns points only;
  the answer values the platform echoes are dropped on the server and never reach the browser.
- `monitor/vercel.json` and a short `monitor/README.md` (deploy and token-rotation commands).

The token lives only in Vercel's encrypted environment, never in the repo or the page. Because the link is public,
the page shows our quality, cost and time to anyone who has the URL; it shows no answer or site values.

## The page (kept to four parts)

1. **Verdict, one sentence at the top:** "Build 14 is better than build 13" (or worse, or about the same), with the
   three numbers behind it: runs at full quality (e.g. 4 of 4 against 3 of 4), median time, median cost. Order of
   judgement: quality first, then cost × time; differences under 5 % count as the same. Builds with fewer than 2
   finished runs say "too few runs yet" instead of a verdict.
2. **Running now:** one row per run in flight: build, elapsed, calls, cost so far.
3. **Builds table, newest first** (the Atira leaderboard layout): Build, Runs, Quality, Time, Cost, Cost × time,
   and a "Progression" column in Atira's style (`100 → 100 → 5 → 100`) so an unstable build is obvious. An arrow next
   to each number shows better or worse than the build before.
4. **Runs of a build** (click a row): each run with status, quality, time, cost, calls and a link to the platform run
   page. Ticking two runs shows the points per field that differ.

Builds are numbered in order of first appearance (Build 1, 2, …) with the short package hash beside them, plus the
platform package label when one exists.

## Design, taken from the Atira site

White paper background, hairline rules, no cards or shadows. Tokens read from their stylesheet: ink `#121311`, rule
`#e3e4e0`, wash `#f7f7f5`, accent `#1d3098`; Geist for text, Geist Mono for numbers and the small uppercase column
labels (11 px, 0.08em tracking), Newsreader serif for the page title; tabular numbers, 13 px table text. Their go,
warn and stop colours mark better, unstable and worse. The page is titled as our team's monitor, not as Atira's.

## Deploying

The Vercel CLI is not installed and nobody is logged in on this machine, so one step needs you:

```sh
! npx vercel login                                   # you, once, in this session
cd monitor && npx vercel link --yes                  # creates the project
atira token | npx vercel env add ATIRA_TOKEN production
npx vercel deploy --prod                             # prints the public URL
```

I run the last three after your login. The deploy uploads only `monitor/`; the private GitHub repo is not connected
to Vercel.

## Files

- New: `monitor/index.html`, `monitor/api/runs.js`, `monitor/api/run.js`, `monitor/vercel.json`, `monitor/README.md`.
- `CLAUDE.md`: one line under "Tracking runs" with the URL and the redeploy command.
- `.gitignore`: add `.vercel/`.
- Untouched: `agent/`, `dev/dashboard.py`, `dev/test-run.sh`, `dev/track.py`.

## Verification

- Before deploying: `npx vercel dev` in `monitor/` with the token in the environment; `curl localhost:3000/api/runs`
  returns only test runs, and its newest ten rows match the MCP `list_runs kind=test` (status, quality, cost, time,
  package).
- The response contains no `answer` key and no token; `api/run` for `run_6fb188024815aa5d` returns points only.
- Two reads 30 s apart while a run is in flight show calls and cost rising.
- Check the verdict by hand against the MCP `compare_runs` for two runs of neighbouring builds.
- After deploying: open the production URL in Chrome, desktop and phone width, and confirm it refreshes.

## Git

Commit on the `monitoring` branch with the team author, subject of at most 50 characters, `-` bullets, no attribution
trailers, nothing under `.claude/`. No push and no PR without asking.

## Context

The team fires many test runs in parallel (133 test runs on the platform, 7 running while planning) and nobody can
see at a glance whether the newest build is better or worse. `dev/dashboard.py` is a static local page, mixes test
and scored runs, and labels only the 5 runs in `experiments/runs.jsonl`.

Requested: a minimal, easy-to-read dashboard for test runs only, live, deployed on Vercel behind a public link, in the
look of the Atira site.

What the atira MCP showed while planning:

- Quality is mostly saturated at 100. The real signal is **reliability per build**: package `6684982fc7e0` scored 5
  once and 100 three times; other builds mix 10, 30.6 or 56 with 100s. So the page compares builds over several runs
  and falls back to time and cost when quality is equal (the platform's own ranking order).
- Running runs already report calls, tokens, cost and elapsed time; every run carries a package SHA-256 to group by.
- The MCP is a local stdio process returning text, so it cannot run inside a Vercel function. The hosted page reads
  the same platform REST API the MCP wraps (`/v1/runs`, `/v1/runs/<id>`); the MCP stays the tool for checking the
  page's numbers and for deep dives from Claude Code.

## What gets built

A new top-level `monitor/` folder (outside `agent/`, so it is never part of the uploaded package), no build step and
no dependencies:

- `monitor/index.html`: the whole page, vanilla JS and inline SVG, re-fetching every 10 s.
- `monitor/api/runs.js`: Node function. Reads `/v1/runs` with the token from the `ATIRA_TOKEN` Vercel secret, keeps
  `kind == "rehearsal"`, and returns only: run id, status, start, duration, quality, eligible, cost, calls, tokens,
  failure class, package hash and label. A 10 s in-memory cache means many viewers cost one platform request.
- `monitor/api/run.js?id=`: points per field for one finished run, for the compare view. It returns points only;
  the answer values the platform echoes are dropped on the server and never reach the browser.
- `monitor/vercel.json` and a short `monitor/README.md` (deploy and token-rotation commands).

The token lives only in Vercel's encrypted environment, never in the repo or the page. Because the link is public,
the page shows our quality, cost and time to anyone who has the URL; it shows no answer or site values.

## The page (kept to four parts)

1. **Verdict, one sentence at the top:** "Build 14 is better than build 13" (or worse, or about the same), with the
   three numbers behind it: runs at full quality (e.g. 4 of 4 against 3 of 4), median time, median cost. Order of
   judgement: quality first, then cost × time; differences under 5 % count as the same. Builds with fewer than 2
   finished runs say "too few runs yet" instead of a verdict.
2. **Running now:** one row per run in flight: build, elapsed, calls, cost so far.
3. **Builds table, newest first** (the Atira leaderboard layout): Build, Runs, Quality, Time, Cost, Cost × time,
   and a "Progression" column in Atira's style (`100 → 100 → 5 → 100`) so an unstable build is obvious. An arrow next
   to each number shows better or worse than the build before.
4. **Runs of a build** (click a row): each run with status, quality, time, cost, calls and a link to the platform run
   page. Ticking two runs shows the points per field that differ.

Builds are numbered in order of first appearance (Build 1, 2, …) with the short package hash beside them, plus the
platform package label when one exists.

## Design, taken from the Atira site

White paper background, hairline rules, no cards or shadows. Tokens read from their stylesheet: ink `#121311`, rule
`#e3e4e0`, wash `#f7f7f5`, accent `#1d3098`; Geist for text, Geist Mono for numbers and the small uppercase column

warn and stop colours mark better, unstable and worse. The page is titled as our team's monitor, not as Atira's.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages
entries.description: Read browser console messages (console.log, console.error, console.warn, etc.) from a specific tab. Useful for debugging JavaScript errors, viewing application logs, or understanding what's happening in the browser console. Returns console messages from the current domain only. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs. IMPORTANT: Always provide a pattern to filter messages - without a pattern, you may get too many irrelevant messages.

tabId.description: Tab ID to read console messages from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

onlyErrors.description: If true, only return error and exception messages. Default is false (return all message types).

clear.description: If true, clear the console messages after reading to avoid duplicates on subsequent calls. Default is false.

pattern.description: Regex pattern to filter console messages. Only messages matching this pattern will be returned (e.g., 'error|warning' to find errors and warnings, 'MyApp' to filter app-specific logs). You should always provide a pattern to avoid getting too many irrelevant messages.

limit.description: Maximum number of messages to return. Defaults to 100. Increase only if you need more results.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__resize_window
entries.description: Resize the current browser window to specified dimensions. Useful for testing responsive designs or setting up specific screen sizes. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to get the window for. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

import asyncio, sys
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright
out = sys.argv[1]
async def main():
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        b = await p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
        errors = []
        page = await b.new_page(viewport={"width": 1280, "height": 900})
        page.on("console", lambda m: errors.append(m.text) if m.type == "error" else None)
        page.on("pageerror", lambda e: errors.append(str(e)))
        await page.goto("http://127.0.0.1:3411/"); await page.wait_for_selector("tr.build")
        await page.wait_for_timeout(1200)
        await page.screenshot(path=out + "/desk.png")
        rows = page.locator("tr.build")
        # open the two newest builds that have finished runs, tick one run in each
        n = await rows.count(); opened = 0
        for i in range(n):
            if "–" not in (await rows.nth(i).locator("td").nth(2).inner_text()) and opened < 2:
                await page.locator("tr.build").nth(i).locator("td").nth(3).click(); opened += 1
                rows = page.locator("tr.build")
        boxes = page.locator("input[data-run]")
        await boxes.first.check()
        await page.locator("input[data-run]").last.check()
        await page.wait_for_timeout(300)
        await page.screenshot(path=out + "/open.png", full_page=False)
        await page.locator("#compare").scroll_into_view_if_needed()
        await page.screenshot(path=out + "/compare.png")
        print("compare:", (await page.locator("#compare").inner_text())[:400])
        m = await b.new_page(viewport={"width": 390, "height": 800})
        await m.goto("http://127.0.0.1:3411/"); await m.wait_for_selector("tr.build"); await m.wait_for_timeout(1000)
        await m.screenshot(path=out + "/phone.png")
        print("phone scroll overflow:", await m.evaluate("document.documentElement.scrollWidth > window.innerWidth"))
        print("errors:", errors)
        await b.close()
asyncio.run(main())
EOF

    async with async_playwright() as p:
        b = await p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
        errors = []
        page = await b.new_page(viewport={"width": 1280, "height": 900})
        page.on("console", lambda m: errors.append(m.text) if m.type == "error" else None)
        page.on("pageerror", lambda e: errors.append(str(e)))
        await page.goto("http://127.0.0.1:3411/"); await page.wait_for_selector("tr.build")
        await page.wait_for_timeout(1200)
        await page.screenshot(path=out + "/desk.png")
        rows = page.locator("tr.build")
        # open the two newest builds that have finished runs, tick one run in each
        n = await rows.count(); opened = 0
        for i in range(n):
            if "–" not in (await rows.nth(i).locator("td").nth(2).inner_text()) and opened < 2:
                await page.locator("tr.build").nth(i).locator("td").nth(3).click(); opened += 1
                rows = page.locator("tr.build")
        boxes = page.locator("input[data-run]")
        await boxes.first.check()
        await page.locator("input[data-run]").last.check()
        await page.wait_for_timeout(300)
        await page.screenshot(path=out + "/open.png", full_page=False)
        await page.locator("#compare").scroll_into_view_if_needed()
        await page.screenshot(path=out + "/compare.png")
        print("compare:", (await page.locator("#compare").inner_text())[:400])
        m = await b.new_page(viewport={"width": 390, "height": 800})
        await m.goto("http://127.0.0.1:3411/"); await m.wait_for_selector("tr.build"); await m.wait_for_timeout(1000)
        await m.screenshot(path=out + "/phone.png")
        print("phone scroll overflow:", await m.evaluate("document.documentElement.scrollWidth > window.innerWidth"))
        print("errors:", errors)
        await b.close()
asyncio.run(main())
